messages.author: a79eb65f0eae8655
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 on its way to CRAN!
parts:
Guys,

I'm sure Hadley got this email as well, but for anyone who didn't: CRAN is forcibly rolling back the package version to v0.8.9 because many packages that depend on ggplot2 (including mine) are breaking. The full text from Uwe Ligges is below:

--- BEGIN EMAIL FROM UWE ---

Dear package maintainers of ggplot2 and Deducer, FourierDescriptors, GGally, HLMdiag, MSG, NeatMap, RcmdrPlugin.KMggplot2, SamplerCompare, SixSigma, TradeStrategyAnalyzer, TripleR, bams, bbmle, bcrm, benchmark, bios2mds, cda, coefplot, directlabels, ez, ezsim, ggcolpairs, ggdendro, ggmap, granovaGG, gsDesign, hyperSpec, nullabor, nvis, pcrcoal, phylosim, planar, pmc, ppstat, rasterVis, robustbase, spef, spikeSlabGAM, tourr, trapezoid, wq,

probably due to yesterday's ggplot2 update on CRAN, we see the other mentioned packages failing now, see e.g.:

http://www.r-project.org/nosvn/R.check/r-devel-windows-ix86+x86_64/Deducer-00check.html

for the first one of the listing above.


Hadley, we asked you several times to sort these things out before uploads to CRAN! Hence we are rolling back the former version of ggplot2 for now until most of these issues are solved prior (!) to the update, please.

Best wishes,

Uwe Ligges

--- END EMAIL FROM UWE ---

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 on its way to CRAN!
parts:
That's really unfortunate. I wonder if this means that it will be impossible to change the public API of a package once it other packages become dependent on it.

I also wonder how the changes should be synchronized. Say that a dependent package uses ggplot2 in one way, but the new version of ggplot2 is changed to do it another way, which breaks the dependent package. Then which package do you change first in CRAN? Either way it would lead to a bad build.

Maybe it's possible to semi-support old behavior but throw warnings about deprecated behavior. I'd guess that some of these breakages are due to the use of scale_x_log2 and scale_x_log, which no longer exist in 0.9.0. Maybe if ggplot had those functions, but just threw warnings about deprecated behavior -- or messages, if warnings break the build of dependent packages.

-Winston

messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 on its way to CRAN!
parts:
I had been checking the main CRAN page for ggplot2 to see when the
windows build was available, and saw the regression to 0.8.9. Now I know
why. Additional comments inline below.

On 1/27/2012 7:53 AM, Winston Chang wrote:
> That's really unfortunate. I wonder if this means that it will be
> impossible to change the public API of a package once it other packages
> become dependent on it.
>
> I also wonder how the changes should be synchronized. Say that a dependent
> package uses ggplot2 in one way, but the new version of ggplot2 is changed
> to do it another way, which breaks the dependent package. Then which
> package do you change first in CRAN? Either way it would lead to a bad
> build.
>
> Maybe it's possible to semi-support old behavior but throw warnings about
> deprecated behavior. I'd guess that some of these breakages are due to the
> use of scale_x_log2 and scale_x_log, which no longer exist in 0.9.0. Maybe
> if ggplot had those functions, but just threw warnings about deprecated
> behavior -- or messages, if warnings break the build of dependent packages.

Using deprecation to phase out behavior is the way to do this.
Effectively, you go through the entire interface (all exported
functions, all of their arguments) [side note: another reason to keep
the number of exported functions as small as possible; partly why I
don't like too many "helper" functions] and make sure that the new
version supports all the functions/arguments. However, for those that
you want to replace, you add a warning() saying that it is deprecated
and will be removed in a future version. A later version can then
change the warning to a stop(), and a version after that can change the
function signature to no longer support the interface. This allows a
transition phase where in the beginning, other code will work but will
produce warnings which can prompt the code to be updated. This would
also have the effect of showing good-faith efforts to get dependent
packages up-to-date rather than suddenly breaking.

Yes, this is more work, but can be aided by the testing to make sure
that warnings (and later errors) are thrown at the right time/right
combination. Basically, planned obsolescence, with warning.

Here is an example:

In ggplot2 0.8.9, the signature for scale_x_continuous is

function (name = NULL, limits = NULL, breaks = NULL, labels = NULL,
trans = NULL, expand = c(0.05, 0), minor_breaks = NULL, formatter =
"scientific",
legend = TRUE, ...)

where ... is ignored.

In ggplot2 0.9.0, the signature for scale_x_continuous is

function (..., expand = c(0.05, 0))

where ... is "common continuous scale parameters: name, breaks, labels,
na.value, limits and trans. See continuous_scale for more details" and
continuous_scale lists names, breaks, minor_breaks, labels, legend,
limits, rescaler, oob, na.value, and trans; aesthetics, scale_name,
palette, and guide are set by the function call itself (and can not be
overridden). Looking at these sets, the only one not supported is
formatter.

Since scale_x_continuous is basically a wrapper anyway,
scale_x_continuous can be changed to:

scale_x_continuous <- function(..., expand = c(0.05, 0), formatter) {
if (!missing(formatter)) {
warning("formatter argument to scale_x_continuous is deprecated.
Formatting of scale labels now handled by providing a function to the
label argument. formatter argument ignored.")
}
continuous_scale(c("x", "xmin", "xmax", "xend", "xintercept"),
"position_c", identity,
..., expand = expand, guide = "none")
}

What you do with it can vary:
* State it is deprecated, at minimum
* Include hint as to what functionality replaces it (even better with
reference to appropriate help page)
* If feasible, map the old functionality to the new. Here, I didn't
bother to even try. Some places it will be easy, some it will be
impossible. If not, stating that the argument is ignored is good

Doing this, things break "softly." They still run, but may give warnings
and may not be exactly what it was in the past. But it also has hints
to what should be done to upgrade it.

This is also testable.

test_that("scale_x_continuous deprecated formatter", {
expect_warning(scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent"))
})

Here is how it looks in action:

qplot(x=runif(40), y=sample(40)) +
scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")


> qplot(x=runif(40), y=sample(40)) +
+ scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")
Warning message:
In scale_x_continuous(formatter = "percent") :
formatter argument to scale_x_continuous is deprecated. Formatting of
scale labels now handled by providing a function to the label argument.
formatter argument ignored.

But a plot is made. Not identical to what you get in 0.8.9, but it
doesn't break. Without this, you get

> qplot(x=runif(40), y=sample(40)) +
+ scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")
Error in continuous_scale(c("x", "xmin", "xmax", "xend", "xintercept"), :
unused argument(s) (formatter = "percent")


Functions that were removed get re-stubbed, again with a warning.

scale_x_log1p <- function(...) {
warning("scale_x_log1p is deprecated. Use
scale_x_continuous(trans=log1p_trans()) where log1p_trans is in the
scales package")
scale_x_continuous(..., trans=log1p_trans())
}


> qplot(x=rexp(40,0.001), y=sample(40)) +
+ scale_x_log1p()
Warning message:
In scale_x_log1p() :
scale_x_log1p is deprecated. Use
scale_x_continuous(trans=log1p_trans()) where log1p_trans is in the
scales package

These could all be put in a single deprecated stubs file.


At some future version, warning can be changed to stop and bridging code
can be removed (and expect_warning changed to expect_error). At a
version after that, the signature can be altered and the checks removed
entirely (whether tests remain is optional); anything that would break
should already have broken by then. If it has not been fixed at that
point, it's not going to be. But the authors have been given plenty of
chance to fix it.


If this is is the approach to take, here is something to help get started.

(in a session with ggplot2 0.8.9):

gg089funs <- ls("package:ggplot2")
names(gg089funs) <- gg089funs
gg089args <- llply(gg089funs, function(f) {names(formals(get(f)))})
#save(gg089funs, gg089args, file="gg089.RData")

(in a session with ggplot2 0.9.0):

gg090funs <- ls("package:ggplot2")
names(gg090funs) <- gg090funs
gg090args <- llply(gg090funs, function(f) {names(formals(get(f)))})
#load("gg089.RData")


missingfuns <- setdiff(gg089funs, gg090funs)
commonfuns <- intersect(gg089funs, gg090funs)
diffargs <- list()
for (fun in commonfuns) {
dff <- setdiff(gg089args[[fun]], gg090args[[fun]])
if (length(dff) != 0) {
diffargs[[fun]] <- dff
}
}

messages.author: dc06d729e023580a
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 on its way to CRAN!
parts:
> Using deprecation to phase out behavior is the way to do this. Effectively,
> you go through the entire interface (all exported functions, all of their
> arguments) [side note: another reason to keep the number of exported
> functions as small as possible; partly why I don't like too many "helper"
> functions] and make sure that the new version supports all the
> functions/arguments. However, for those that you want to replace, you add a
> warning() saying that it is deprecated and will be removed in a future
> version.  A later version can then change the warning to a stop(), and a
> version after that can change the function signature to no longer support
> the interface.  This allows a transition phase where in the beginning, other
> code will work but will produce warnings which can prompt the code to be
> updated.  This would also have the effect of showing good-faith efforts to
> get dependent packages up-to-date rather than suddenly breaking.

Unfortunately I barely have the resources to update ggplot2, let along
update it in a way that guarantees not to break existing code.

> Yes, this is more work, but can be aided by the testing to make sure that
> warnings (and later errors) are thrown at the right time/right combination.
> Basically, planned obsolescence, with warning.

I barely have any tests that cover desired functionality, let alone
ensuring it's backward compatible :(

At this point I'm leaning towards just making it ggplot3. Otherwise
there's not going to be a ggplotx release before June at the minimum.

Hadley


--

Department of Statistics / Rice University

programming/software engineering I've learned.

>> warnings (and later errors) are thrown at the right time/right combination.
>> Basically, planned obsolescence, with warning.

Good thing there is "a testing package specifically tailored for R
that's fun, flexible and easy to set up." ;)

(Going forward, of course.)

> At this point I'm leaning towards just making it ggplot3. Otherwise
> there's not going to be a ggplotx release before June at the minimum.

Might I suggest ggplot2b rather than ggplot3? Much of what is
understood about ggplot2 still is valid, and that will (possibly) create
less naming confusion (since the mailing lists, etc., would maintain the
"ggplot2" naming, I assume). Still technically different such that you
don't have to worry about the backward compatibility problems on CRAN.
I'd also keep it with the 0.9.0 version number.

It would be a shame to have to wait until June. Once or twice a week
there are posts with questions where the answer is "it's fixed in the
development version."

> Hadley

smaller packages, I hope the test coverage will improve. It's also
been great to have other developers start contributing code and tests

the reason I'm trying to write up my thoughts about R development best

> I'm willing to take a shot at adding in code to let the dependent packages
> build and keep the CRAN people happy. (This isn't to say that the dependent
> packages will necessarily work correctly, though.)

I guess I'm not sure how worthwhile this is.    But see my other
request - let's see what other package authors mainly struggle with,
and selectively fix problems as they arise.

Hopefully we won't run issues where someone fixes a package to work with 0.9.0, thus breaking the build with 0.8.9, and then CRAN doesn't accept their package because it doesn't work with the "current" version of ggplot2.

It might also help to pass along Dennis's transition guide draft - there's a good chance it covers some of the issues.

-Winston

I had a similar thought - it needs to be cleaned up a bit before
releasing it publicly, though. If many of the problems have to do with
the loss of some of the scale_ functions, then we probably need to put
more examples of the use of scales in 0.9.0 in the document. I could
see a release by the middle of next week (on the ggplot2 wiki?) if I
can get some help in tidying up some of the prose and making sure that
the essential changes are covered.

I don't really know how other package authors use ggplot2 and where
it's breaking, so if something is broken and not covered in the
transition guide, then we need to know what needs to be fixed so that
it can be covered in the guide.

Dennis
